diagrams.name: path-p63-skin-cancer
diagrams.title: Skin cancer: healthy epidermis and three cancer types

cloze.text: Examples of a {{c1::macule}}: freckle, amalgam tattoo in the oral mucosa, petechiae.
Examples of a {{c1::plaque}}: oral leukoplakia, psoriasis plaque, oral hairy leukoplakia.
Examples of a {{c1::pustule}}: acne pimple, impetigo lesion, periapical abscess draining on the gums.
Examples of a {{c1::vesicle}}: herpes simplex blister on the lip, chickenpox blister.
Examples of a {{c1::bulla}}: bullous pemphigoid skin blisters, second-degree burn blister.
Examples of a {{c1::papule}}: skin mole (nevus), Fordyce granule, lichen planus bump, skin tag.
Examples of a {{c1::nodule}}: lymph nodules, fibroma, lipoma, cyst.
Describing a lesion — color: red, white, yellow, blue, black, brown, or mixed. Shape/form: round, oval, irregular, flat, {{c1::raised}}, or {{c2::depressed}}.
Describing a lesion — {{c1::content}} (what is inside): clear fluid (serum, mucin), yellow pus, or solid tissue.
Describing a lesion — lesion size is measured in {{c1::millimeters (mm) or centimeters (cm)}}.
Describing a lesion — texture terms: smooth, rough, {{c1::papillary}}, cauliflower-like, {{c2::verrucous}}, corrugated, crusted, or ulcerated.
Describing a lesion — location: the {{c1::precise anatomical site}} (e.g., buccal mucosa, tongue, palate, gingiva).
Describing a lesion — border/margin: {{c1::well-defined}} (sharp) or {{c2::ill-defined}} (diffuse).
Describing a lesion — consistency (on palpation): soft, firm, {{c1::fluctuant}} (fluid-filled), or hard.
Minor aphthous ulcer — color: {{c1::red border}} with a {{c2::yellowish-white base}}.
Minor aphthous ulcer — content: {{c1::no fluid; exposed connective tissue}} (solid base).
Minor aphthous ulcer — texture: {{c1::rough, necrotic}} surface; shape: {{c2::round or oval depression}}.
Minor aphthous ulcer — location: {{c1::labial mucosa, buccal mucosa, ventral tongue}}.
Minor aphthous ulcer — border: well-defined {{c1::red halo}} around the lesion; consistency: soft at the center, slightly {{c2::tender}} on palpation.
Fordyce granules are clusters of {{c1::ectopic sebaceous (oil) glands}}.
cloze.extra: Ectopic = in an abnormal place or pattern. WakeUpMemory: "Fordyce = Face oil dots."

cloze.text: Fordyce granules are found mostly on the {{c1::lips}} and {{c2::buccal mucosa}}.
Fordyce granules appear as clusters of tiny {{c1::yellow}} lobules.
An {{c1::exostosis}} is a benign bony overgrowth on the {{c2::buccal (outer)}} surface of the maxilla or mandible.
{{c1::Torus palatinus}} (maxillary torus) appears near the {{c2::midline of the hard palate}}.
Mandibular tori appear on the {{c1::lingual}} aspect of the mandible in the {{c2::premolar}} region; usually {{c3::bilateral}}, lobulated, or nodular.
cloze.extra: Tori is the plural of torus.

cloze.text: On a radiograph, a large torus may appear as a {{c1::radiopaque}} mass.
Melanin pigmentation is caused by {{c1::increased melanin production}} in the oral mucosa.
Melanin pigmentation is common on the {{c1::gingiva}} and {{c2::labial mucosa}}, most often in {{c3::dark-skinned}} individuals.
Melanin pigmentation appears as flat, dark {{c1::macules}}; borders may be well-defined or diffuse.
Lingual varicosities are enlarged, dilated veins on the {{c1::ventral surface and sides}} of the tongue.
Lingual varicosities appear as {{c1::purple or blue}}, enlarged vessels visible under the tongue; they are asymptomatic.
Linea alba is a {{c1::white line}} on the buccal mucosa at the level where the upper and lower teeth meet, following the {{c2::occlusal plane}}.
Linea alba appears as a white, raised, well-defined line, often {{c1::bilateral}}; it is asymptomatic.
Leukoedema is a generalized opalescent or milky-white appearance of the buccal mucosa caused by {{c1::intracellular edema in the spinous cell layer}}.
Leukoedema is a bilateral, diffuse, gray-white opalescent surface with a wrinkled texture that {{c1::diminishes when stretched}}.
Leukoedema is most often seen on the {{c1::buccal mucosa}} and is more common in {{c2::Black adults}} and {{c3::smokers}}; it is asymptomatic.
The thyroid originates at the base of the tongue near the {{c1::foramen cecum}} around the {{c2::4th}} week and descends to its final position in the neck by the {{c3::7th}} week.
A lingual thyroid nodule is located on the {{c1::midline of the dorsal tongue}}, behind the circumvallate papillae, near the foramen cecum.
A lingual thyroid is a smooth, nodular mass that is usually asymptomatic but may interfere with {{c1::swallowing, speech, or breathing}} if large.

An amalgam tattoo is a benign discoloration of the mucosa due to accidental {{c1::implantation of amalgam (silver filling)}} during dental procedures; it is commonly found near a {{c2::restoration site}}.
An amalgam tattoo is a flat, {{c1::blue-gray}} discoloration with well-defined borders; it may show {{c2::radiopaque flecks}} on a radiograph.
Tumors are staged by malignancy potential using the {{c1::TNM}} staging system ({{c2::Tumor, Node, Metastasis}}); higher stages mean a {{c3::worse}} prognosis.
A {{c1::benign}} tumor remains localized and does not invade surrounding tissues (no metastasis).
A {{c1::malignant}} tumor invades and destroys surrounding tissues and can metastasize to distant sites.
cloze.extra: Cancer is synonymous with malignancy.

cloze.text: Tumor names end with {{c1::-oma}}.
Benign tumor of fat = {{c1::lipoma}}.
Benign tumor of salivary glands = {{c1::adenoma}}.
Benign tumor of bone = {{c1::osteoma}}.
Benign tumor of muscle = {{c1::rhabdomyoma}}.
Benign tumor of squamous epithelium = {{c1::papilloma}}.
Malignant tumor of epithelium = {{c1::carcinoma}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: SArcoma, MElanoma, CARcinoma are cancerous — SA ME CAR.

cloze.text: Malignant tumor of connective tissue = {{c1::sarcoma}}.
cloze.extra: SA ME CAR = sarcoma, melanoma, carcinoma are cancerous.

cloze.text: Malignant tumor of melanocytes = {{c1::melanoma}}.
cloze.extra: SA ME CAR = sarcoma, melanoma, carcinoma are cancerous.

cloze.text: Oral squamous papilloma is a benign tumor of {{c1::squamous epithelium}} related to {{c2::HPV types 6 and 11}} (low-risk types).
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: papilloma means "small projections" in Latin — hence its finger-like projections.

cloze.text: Oral papilloma is most common on the {{c1::soft palate, uvula, tongue, or lips}}.
Oral papilloma is a small, exophytic, pedunculated or sessile mass with a {{c1::cauliflower-like or finger-like}} surface.
An irritation fibroma is a benign {{c1::fibrous}} overgrowth caused by {{c2::chronic irritation}} (e.g., cheek biting, friction from sharp teeth).
An irritation fibroma is most often found on the {{c1::buccal mucosa}}.
An irritation fibroma appears as a small, firm, smooth, light pink, elevated {{c1::nodule}}.
A lipoma is a benign tumor of mature {{c1::fat}} cells, {{c2::rare}} in the oral cavity but common elsewhere in the body.
In the mouth, a lipoma is most common on the {{c1::buccal mucosa or vestibule}}.
A lipoma is a soft, smooth, {{c1::yellowish}}, fluctuant submucosal mass, usually under {{c2::3 cm}}.
Neurofibromas are benign tumors derived from {{c1::nerve}} tissue; they involve multiple cell types ({{c2::Schwann cells and fibroblasts}}) and are {{c3::diffuse}}.
Multiple neurofibromas may be a sign of {{c1::neurofibromatosis type 1}} ({{c2::von Recklinghausen}} disease), a genetic disorder.
cloze.extra: Did you know: actor Adam Pearson has neurofibromatosis; his twin brother is less visibly affected, showing the variable expression of the condition.

cloze.text: Oral neurofibromas are most common on the {{c1::tongue or buccal mucosa}}.
Neurofibromatosis: slow-growing, soft, painless nodules plus {{c1::café au lait spots}} (flat, light-brown skin patches).
{{c1::Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)}} is the most common primary malignancy of the oral cavity.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: SCC → "SCO = Scary Cancer in the Oral cavity."

cloze.text: Oral SCC arises from {{c1::squamous epithelium}} — flat epithelial cells that make up most of the epidermis and line the entire oral cavity.
Oral SCC is common on the {{c1::ventrolateral tongue}}, {{c2::floor of the mouth}}, soft palate, tonsillar pillar, and {{c3::lower lip}} (from sun exposure).
Risk factors for oral SCC: {{c1::tobacco}} use, {{c2::alcohol}} consumption, and {{c3::sun}} exposure.
Oral SCC appears as a non-healing ulcer, exophytic mass, or leukoplakic/erythroplakic lesion with {{c1::indurated (firm)}} borders.
Basal cell carcinoma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of {{c2::basal cells}} in the deepest layer of the epidermis.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: think basal = beach — a lot of sun.

cloze.text: Basal cell carcinoma occurs on {{c1::sun-exposed skin}} (face, scalp, ears) and {{c2::does not occur intraorally}}.
Basal cell carcinoma appears as a non-healing ulcer with {{c1::rolled borders}} and a central depression, often with visible blood vessels ({{c2::telangiectasia}}).
Melanoma is a malignant tumor of {{c1::melanocytes}} (pigment-producing cells).
Melanoma occurs mainly on the skin; intraoral melanomas are very rare and most common on the {{c1::palate or gingiva}}.
Melanoma appears as a dark lesion with {{c1::irregular}} borders; it may also be pink, red, or white.
Sarcomas are malignant tumors of {{c1::connective tissue}} origin, including bone, muscle, and blood vessels.
Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone tumor, often presenting as {{c1::painful}} swelling, tooth mobility, or toothache.
On a radiograph, osteosarcoma shows a {{c1::"sunburst"}} radiopaque pattern due to spiculated bone formation.
Osteosarcoma is common in {{c1::young adults}} and often affects the {{c2::posterior mandible}}.
Kaposi sarcoma is a {{c1::vascular}} malignancy associated with {{c2::HHV-8}} (human herpesvirus 8), mostly in {{c3::immunocompromised}} patients (e.g., HIV/AIDS).
Kaposi sarcoma appears as red, purple, or bluish plaques or nodules, especially on the {{c1::palate or gingiva}}.
Treatment of Kaposi sarcoma may involve {{c1::antiretroviral therapy}}, radiation, or chemotherapy.
Leukoplakia is a {{c1::white patch}} or plaque on the oral mucosa that {{c2::cannot be rubbed off}} and cannot be clinically or histologically diagnosed as any other disease.
Leukoplakia is common on the buccal mucosa, tongue, floor of the mouth, and gingiva; risk factors are {{c1::tobacco}}, {{c2::alcohol}}, and {{c3::chronic irritation}}.
Leukoplakia is asymptomatic but requires a {{c1::biopsy}} to rule out malignancy.
Erythroplakia is a {{c1::red patch}} on the oral mucosa that cannot be attributed to any other condition.
Erythroplakia is most common on the {{c1::floor of the mouth}}, ventral tongue, and soft palate.
Erythroplakia carries a {{c1::higher}} risk of malignant transformation than leukoplakia.
Erythroplakia appears {{c1::velvety red}} and well-demarcated, often with no surface irregularities; it is asymptomatic — biopsy to rule out malignancy.
Solar (actinic) cheilitis is a {{c1::precancerous}} condition caused by chronic {{c2::sun (UV) exposure}}, especially in fair-skinned individuals.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: cheilitis = Greek "cheilos" (lip) + "-itis" (inflammation).

cloze.text: Solar cheilitis primarily affects the {{c1::lower lip}} and vermilion border.
Solar cheilitis appears as pale, dry, crusted, or fissured mucosa with a {{c1::blurred lip-skin junction}}.
Solar cheilitis is asymptomatic; a {{c1::biopsy}} is recommended.
Ameloblastoma is a {{c1::benign}}, slow-growing, locally aggressive {{c2::odontogenic}} tumor from remnants of the {{c3::dental lamina}}.
Ameloblastoma is most common in the {{c1::posterior mandible}}, especially the {{c2::ramus}} (about 80% of cases).
Radiographically, ameloblastoma is a {{c1::multilocular}} radiolucency with a {{c2::soap bubble or honeycomb}} appearance.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: ameloBLAST → celebration → champagne → bubbles → soap bubble appearance.

cloze.text: Ameloblastoma causes painless swelling, gradual {{c1::bone expansion}}, facial asymmetry, and possible tooth displacement or {{c2::root resorption}}.
The nasopalatine cyst is a cyst within the {{c1::nasopalatine canal}}, near the midline of the anterior palate between or behind the {{c2::maxillary central incisors}}.
Radiographically, the nasopalatine cyst is a radiolucent, {{c1::heart-shaped}} lesion near the apices of the central incisors.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: I "heart" (love) naps — nasopalatine.

cloze.text: A nasopalatine cyst may present as a small pink bulge on the palate in the {{c1::incisive papilla}} area.
The median palatine cyst is a {{c1::non-odontogenic developmental}} cyst in the midline of the {{c2::posterior hard palate}} (more posterior than the nasopalatine cyst).
Radiographically, the median palatine cyst is a well-defined {{c1::unilocular}} radiolucency; asymptomatic, removal if needed.
The globulomaxillary cyst is a non-odontogenic developmental cyst between the roots of the {{c1::maxillary lateral incisor and canine}}.
cloze.extra: Historically thought to arise from fusion of the globular and maxillary processes.

cloze.text: Radiographically, the globulomaxillary cyst is a well-defined, {{c1::pear-shaped}} radiolucency.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: think of a canine (dog) eating a pear.

cloze.text: A globulomaxillary cyst is asymptomatic but can cause root {{c1::divergence}}; removal if needed.
The static bone cyst (Stafne bone defect) is a {{c1::pseudocyst}}: a developmental bone depression in the posterior mandible, often containing {{c2::salivary gland tissue}}.
The static bone cyst is located {{c1::below the mandibular canal}}, typically near the {{c2::angle of the mandible}}.
Radiographically, the static bone cyst is a well-defined radiolucent area; it is asymptomatic and {{c1::non-expansile}}, and needs {{c2::no treatment}}.
cloze.extra: "Static" = stable, as the name suggests.

cloze.text: The simple (traumatic) bone cyst is a cavity inside the bone, typically without an epithelial lining, making it a {{c1::pseudocyst}}.
The simple bone cyst is commonly in the {{c1::posterior mandible}} of {{c2::adolescents and young adults}}.
Radiographically, the simple bone cyst is a well-defined radiolucency with {{c1::scalloping}} between the roots of {{c2::vital}} teeth.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: simple bone cyst = scalloped — scallops with a simple dash of salt and pepper.

cloze.text: The simple bone cyst is often linked to prior {{c1::trauma}}; it is asymptomatic and needs no treatment.
The aneurysmal bone cyst is a {{c1::pseudocyst}} filled with {{c2::blood-filled spaces}}, leading to rapid bone expansion and noticeable facial swelling.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: aneurysm means "blood-filled swelling" — think of a honeycomb filled with blood.

cloze.text: The aneurysmal bone cyst is most common in the {{c1::mandible}} and typically affects {{c2::children and young adults}}.
Radiographically, the aneurysmal bone cyst is a multilocular radiolucency with a {{c1::honeycomb or soap bubble}} pattern.
Cherubism is a {{c1::hereditary}} condition in which the bone of the mandible is replaced by excessive {{c2::fibrous tissue}}.
Cherubism mostly affects the {{c1::posterior mandible}}; the swelling is often {{c2::symmetrical (bilateral)}}.
Cherubism causes {{c1::painless}}, progressive jaw enlargement giving a "cherubic" facial appearance.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: a cherub is a sweet, innocent-looking child with plump cheeks — bilateral jaw swelling creates full, rounded cheeks.

cloze.text: Dental impact of cherubism: premature loss of {{c1::primary}} teeth and delayed or failed eruption of {{c2::permanent}} teeth.
Cherubism often {{c1::stabilizes after puberty}}; surgeries if needed.
Fibrous dysplasia is a genetic condition affecting {{c1::bone and pigment cells}}: bone is replaced by abnormal fibrous connective tissue with calcifications, weakening the bone.
cloze.extra: The book pictures café au lait spots with this condition.

cloze.text: Fibrous dysplasia is common in the {{c1::maxilla}}; it can also involve the skull, clavicles, or long bones.
Fibrous dysplasia causes bone enlargement with a {{c1::"ground glass"}} radiopacity.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: ground glass → fiberglass (glass fibers in resin).

cloze.text: Fibrous dysplasia is {{c1::painless}} and slow-growing; surgeries if needed.
Paget disease ({{c1::osteitis deformans}}) is a chronic metabolic bone disorder with abnormal cycles of bone {{c2::resorption, repair, and remineralization}}.
Paget disease can affect the skull, jaws, and other bones; it is most common in {{c1::men over 50}}.
Paget disease shows a {{c1::"cotton-wool"}} radiopacity (patchy, disorganized, fluffy) due to irregular bone deposition.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Paget sounds like pajama — pajamas made of cotton or wool.

cloze.text: Multiple myeloma is a {{c1::malignant}} tumor of {{c2::plasma cells}} that originates in the {{c3::bone marrow}}, commonly affecting older adults.
cloze.extra: Myelo = bone marrow.

cloze.text: Multiple myeloma often involves the skull, spine, or jaw bones and appears as {{c1::punched-out}} radiolucencies.
Symptoms of multiple myeloma: pain, fatigue, anemia, and {{c1::renal}} issues due to abnormal proteins.

basic.back: A flat area of altered color, with no elevation or depression
basic.extra: Compare to a papule: papules are raised, macules are completely flat.

basic.back: A slightly raised, broad, flat-topped lesion
basic.extra: Compare to a papule: plaques are broad and flat-topped; papules are small and rounded.

basic.back: A pus-filled lesion of any size, containing yellow pus
basic.extra: Compare to a papule: papules are solid, pustules have pus.

basic.back: A lesion with a broad base — base wider than the top
A lesion on a narrow stalk (pedicle) — base smaller than the top
A fluid-filled blister ≤ 5 mm, containing serum or mucin
basic.extra: Compare to a bulla: both are fluid-filled, but a bulla is larger (> 5 mm).

basic.back: A fluid-filled blister > 5 mm, containing serum or mucin
basic.extra: Compare to a vesicle: same fluid type, just larger.

basic.back: A small solid raised lesion ≤ 5 mm, made of tissue
basic.extra: Compare to a pustule: same size range, but papules contain solid tissue, not pus.

basic.back: A solid raised lesion > 5 mm, made of tissue
basic.extra: Compare to a papule: nodules are larger, but both are solid.

basic.back: Only if they interfere with speech, prosthetic appliances, or swallowing.
Asymptomatic. Biopsy only if melanoma (cancer) is suspected.
Age-related loss of elasticity in the venous walls, leading to dilated, tortuous veins.
Frictional irritation from habits such as cheek biting, bruxism, or pressure from the teeth.

basic.front: What causes a lingual thyroid nodule?
basic.back: Incomplete migration of the thyroid during embryonic development, leaving ectopic thyroid tissue on the tongue.
Asymptomatic; no treatment needed. A biopsy may be considered to rule out melanoma.
An abnormal growth of tissue resulting from uncontrolled, excessive cell proliferation

basic.front: Why can an oral papilloma be white or pink?
basic.back: White if keratinized, pink if non-keratinized.
Slow-growing, sharply demarcated, asymptomatic and non-invasive; treated by surgical excision.
Asymptomatic and stable; no treatment needed — remove the source of irritation.

basic.front: Frictional keratosis vs irritation fibroma — both are reactive lesions from chronic irritation. How do they differ?
basic.back:
Frictional keratosis = EPITHELIAL response → white, flat, rough.
Irritation fibroma = CONNECTIVE TISSUE response → pink, raised, smooth.
Slow-growing, painless, mobile on palpation; harmless — surgical removal if needed.

basic.front: Neurofibroma vs schwannoma — cell origin and capsule?
basic.back:
Neurofibroma: Schwann cells + fibroblasts, diffuse (not encapsulated).
Schwannoma: Schwann cells only, encapsulated.
Asymptomatic; surgical removal may be considered.

basic.front: Oral SCC: symptoms early on, and why it matters?
basic.back: Asymptomatic early, but it can invade surrounding tissues.

basic.front: Basal cell carcinoma: behavior and treatment?
basic.back: Slow-growing and rarely metastasizes, but can cause significant local destruction. Remove surgically.

basic.front: Why is the prognosis of melanoma poor?
basic.back: It is asymptomatic in early stages, so detection is late, and it progresses rapidly.

basic.front: Is leukoplakia a diagnosis of cancer?
basic.back: No — it is a clinical description: a white patch that cannot be wiped off and cannot be classified as any other disease. Most leukoplakias are benign.

basic.front: What causes solar cheilitis — friction, trauma, or UV?
basic.back: Cumulative UV damage (not friction or trauma).
Asymptomatic in early stages. Surgical excision; recurrence is common.

basic.front: Nasopalatine cyst: are the adjacent teeth vital? Treatment?
basic.back: Yes — asymptomatic and the teeth are vital. Removal if needed.

basic.front: What makes a lesion a true cyst vs a pseudocyst?
basic.back: A true cyst is a cavity lined by epithelium (usually filled with fluid, semi-fluid, or gas). A pseudocyst looks like a cyst but lacks the epithelial lining.

basic.front: Aneurysmal bone cyst: symptoms and treatment?
basic.back: Rapid expansion (despite being benign) may cause pain or facial asymmetry. Surgical curettage; recurrence is possible.

basic.front: Paget disease: signs relevant to dentistry?
basic.back: Bone pain, jaw enlargement, increased spacing of teeth; dentures may no longer fit due to jaw changes. Treatment is needed.

mcq.question: A patient has a flat, brown, 3-mm area of discoloration on the buccal mucosa with no elevation. How is it best described?
mcq.explanation: A macule is a flat area of altered color with no elevation or depression. A papule is the best distractor but is raised and solid.

mcq.question: A clear, fluid-filled blister measuring 8 mm is seen on the lip. Which term describes it?
mcq.explanation: A bulla is a fluid-filled blister > 5 mm. A vesicle contains the same fluid (serum or mucin) but is ≤ 5 mm; a pustule contains yellow pus.

mcq.question: A 45-year-old Black patient who smokes has a bilateral, diffuse, gray-white opalescent buccal mucosa. The whiteness fades when the cheek is stretched. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Leukoedema is a gray-white opalescent buccal mucosa that diminishes when stretched; more common in Black adults and smokers. Leukoplakia does not disappear on stretching and cannot be wiped off; it needs a biopsy.

mcq.question: Clusters of tiny yellow lobules are seen on the buccal mucosa of an otherwise healthy adult. These are
mcq.explanation: Fordyce granules are ectopic sebaceous (oil) glands that look like tiny yellow lobules on the lips and buccal mucosa; over 80% of adults have them. Melanin pigmentation is flat and dark, not yellow.

mcq.question: A flat, blue-gray, well-defined lesion is found on the gingiva next to a large amalgam restoration. A radiograph shows tiny radiopaque flecks in the area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: An amalgam tattoo is a flat blue-gray discoloration near a restoration, often with radiopaque flecks on the radiograph. Melanoma has irregular borders and no radiopaque flecks; a biopsy may be done to rule it out.

mcq.question: A patient who habitually bites her cheek has a firm, smooth, light-pink, raised nodule on the buccal mucosa at the occlusal plane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Irritation fibroma is a connective-tissue response to chronic irritation: pink, raised, smooth, firm. Frictional keratosis is an epithelial response: white, flat, rough. A lipoma is soft and yellowish.

mcq.question: Which skin cancer does NOT occur intraorally?
mcq.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma occurs on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, ears) and does not occur intraorally. Melanoma is rare in the mouth but does occur, mostly on the palate or gingiva.

mcq.question: A patient with HIV/AIDS has several purple nodules on the hard palate. Which virus is associated with the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Purple/red/bluish palatal plaques or nodules in an immunocompromised patient suggest Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular malignancy associated with HHV-8. HPV 6 and 11 are linked to the benign squamous papilloma.

mcq.question: Which oral lesion carries the HIGHEST risk of malignant transformation?
mcq.explanation: Erythroplakia (velvety red patch) has a higher risk of malignant transformation than leukoplakia. Leukoedema and linea alba are normal variants.

mcq.question: A well-defined, pear-shaped radiolucency is seen between the roots of the maxillary lateral incisor and canine, which are diverging. The teeth are vital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: The globulomaxillary cyst is a pear-shaped radiolucency between the maxillary lateral incisor and canine and can cause root divergence. The nasopalatine cyst is heart-shaped and sits between the central incisors.

mcq.question: A routine panoramic image shows a well-defined radiolucency below the mandibular canal near the angle of the mandible. It has not changed in size over several years. What is the appropriate management?
mcq.explanation: This is a static bone cyst (Stafne defect): a non-expansile pseudocyst, often containing salivary gland tissue, that needs no treatment. Curettage is the treatment for the aneurysmal bone cyst.

mcq.question: A 60-year-old man reports bone pain, and his complete denture no longer fits. Radiographs show patchy, fluffy "cotton-wool" radiopacities in the jaws. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Paget disease (osteitis deformans) is most common in men over 50, enlarges the jaws (dentures stop fitting, teeth space out) and shows a cotton-wool radiopacity. Fibrous dysplasia is painless and shows a ground-glass radiopacity.

mcq.question: A 9-year-old has painless, symmetrical bilateral enlargement of the posterior mandible, early loss of primary teeth and delayed eruption of permanent teeth. A sibling had the same condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Cherubism is hereditary, affects children under 20, causes painless bilateral posterior mandibular enlargement and disrupts tooth eruption; it often stabilizes after puberty. An aneurysmal bone cyst expands rapidly and may be painful and asymmetric.
